extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of political communication and democratic theory (journalists, political leaders, social scientists)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and explains principles about how leaders, symbols, and organizational 'machines' shape mass opinion and collective action. Focuses on the mechanisms by which authority, symbols, hierarchy, and publicity influence what publics think and do.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbol adoption via authoritative introducers
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbols take root in a person's mind because they are 'planted there by another human being whom we recognize as authoritative.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If symbols are introduced by congenial and important people they become congenial and important to us; later we may retroactively call the symbol-waver authoritative. Example: national flags, totem poles, or political slogans gain force because trusted persons present them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on trustworthy reporters when truth is inaccessible
rubrics_metrics.description: When facts are out of sight people choose between 'trustworthy and untrustworthy reporters' rather than between true and false accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because ordinary citizens lack expertise or access to all facts, they evaluate sources for trustworthiness; this shapes which accounts circulate and become accepted. The literature of psychoanalysis is suggested for hypotheses about how trust spreads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical selection of authority by accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Although theoretically one should select the most expert source, in practice people choose accessible authorities — 'the people who are at the head of affairs' like parents, teachers, and influential acquaintances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts may be hard to identify or consult; therefore position, visibility, and social relation (parent, teacher, boss) often determine who becomes authoritative, regardless of actual expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of a 'machine' (hierarchy) for collective action
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass cooperation in complex affairs requires a small, organized hierarchy (a 'machine'); a public as such can at most say Yes or No, but cannot itself devise, negotiate, or administer complex policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: legislatures, parties, trade unions, armies — all have inner circles that decide and administer. Without such organization, mass action is limited to simple refusals or approvals (strikes, boycotts, votes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Machines rely on systems of privileges to bind members
rubrics_metrics.description: What holds a machine together is a system of privileges — patronage, jobs, publicity, rank — which create insiders and outsiders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Privileges vary by institution (nepotism, military rank, jobs). Abolishing privileges can break a particular machine, but new hierarchies will reappear because relative privilege and the desire for insider status persist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaders cultivate symbols to conserve unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful leaders 'cultivate the symbols which organize his following' because symbols merge differences and conserve unity among diverse followers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Symbols discharge emotion at a common target and blot out idiosyncratic ideas; leaders depend on them to mobilize crowds and to avoid disruptive probing or 'destructive criticism.' Examples: national flags, ritual, or iconic rhetoric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbols as double-edged instruments (solidarity and exploitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbols enable common action but also allow a few to deflect criticism, seduce followers, and exploit them for ends they do not understand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While symbols can be necessary for quick coordinated action, they can also mask personal intentions and be used to mobilize people toward objectives chosen by leaders rather than understood by followers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for secrecy and controlled information in crises
rubrics_metrics.description: In emergencies leaders may withhold information (e.g., casualty lists) or limit public debate because open dispute can dissolve unity and impede action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from wartime: withholding casualty totals to preserve morale; leaders keeping dissent within a small circle to avoid panic or disintegration of command. Secrecy can be justified when publicity would be more destructive than wrong decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaders must consider morale when planning policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Every leader must consider not only the merits of a decision but 'its effect on any part of his following whose continued support he requires' — i.e., morale and endurance limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical limits (e.g., casualty tolerance) determine what actions followers will sustain; failure to account for morale can lead to mutinies or revolutions arising from cumulative grievances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaders prefer policies with indirect, distributed costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaders tend to favor programs whose costs are indirect or remote from followers, avoiding policies that immediately impinge on private habits or visible pockets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequently, governments favor long-term debt, indirect taxation, or policies where negative effects are dispersed; visible actors (greedy landlords) are easier political targets than complex systemic reforms (increasing housing supply).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mass decisions are necessarily simple (binary or highly summarized)
rubrics_metrics.description: The practical action a mass can take is generally limited to a simple Yes or No on a presented issue; complex deliberation is rare at mass scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forms claimed to increase directness (initiative, referendum, preferential ballots) still present simplified choices and depend upon pre-formed issues created by organized minorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small groups frame choices for the many
rubrics_metrics.description: A small number of leaders or 'energetic coteries' present concrete choices to the mass (nominations, measures); 'the Many can elect after the Few have nominated.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions like caucuses, conventions, and steering committees formulate issues and filter options; even democratic mechanisms rely on prior agenda-setting by organized groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective policy launching requires emotional/verbal linkage to existing feelings
rubrics_metrics.description: When introducing a new policy, leaders must first 'vocalize the prevalent opinion' and connect the proposed program verbally and emotionally to what is already felt in the mass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategy: identify familiar attitudes via stories, patriotism, grievances; gain trust by appearing to represent common sentiment, then present the plan so it analogically aligns with initial feelings. This is essential where the incidence of policy is remote from followers' immediate experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media and reporters can assume leadership by suggestion
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'reporter' or newspaper proprietor may become the de facto leader because suggestion in news shapes what the mass perceives and how it feels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News often arrives with an 'aura of suggestion' that indicates how readers should feel; this makes media actors powerful in creating the appearance of leadership and in guiding public opinion.
